title: Weighted Event Scoring
explain: Weighted event scoring turns many events of unequal value into one score per item or user: a purchase is worth far more than a view, so you multiply each event by a weight and add them up, usually with time decay so recent activity counts more. Raw counts rank by volume; weighted scores rank by value. (含金量: not every event is worth the same.)
model:
`score = sum over events ( weight(type) x decay(age) )`

Example weights: view = 1, click = 3, add-to-cart = 5, purchase = 10.

**Pipeline:**

```
events ──▶ dedupe by event id ──▶ cap per user/item ──▶ x type weight
       ──▶ x decay(age) ──▶ running score ──▶ top-k
```

**Exponential decay** with half-life `H`: an event of age `t` counts `0.5^(t/H)`. The nice property is that you need only `(score, last_update)` per item and update lazily:

`score = score x 0.5^(dt/H) + weight`

It is the same trick as a lazily refilled [token bucket](#/sd/f/rate-limiter): no event history is rescanned.

**Guardrails:** dampen repeats (`min(count, cap)` or `log(1+count)`), deduplicate because delivery is at-least-once, and treat the weights as product decisions to re-tune against outcomes, not constants.

The result feeds [top-k ranking](#/sd/f/top-k-ranking).

details.q: Why weights instead of raw counts?
details.a: Counts rank by volume, weights rank by value. With view = 1, click = 3, purchase = 10, item A (100 views, 10 clicks, 1 purchase) scores 140 and item B (20 views, 5 clicks, 12 purchases) scores 155. A has far more raw events but B is clearly the better-converting item.

details.q: How do you choose the weights?
details.a: From outcomes: how strongly each event predicts the thing you care about (conversion, retention). Start from ratios that match the funnel, then fit or A/B-test them. They are product decisions that drift as behaviour changes, so revisit them.

details.q: How does time decay work and how do you pick the half-life?
details.a: An event of age `t` is multiplied by `0.5^(t/H)`. With `H` = 7 days, a weight-10 event from 21 days ago (three half-lives) contributes 1.25. Pick `H` from how fast the thing you rank goes stale: hours for trending, weeks for long-term interest.

details.q: Do you have to store every event to compute a decayed score?
details.a: No. Keep `(score, last_update)` and on each new event do `score = score x 0.5^(dt/H) + weight`. For example a score of 8 with `H` = 1 hour, hit by a weight-5 event two hours later, becomes `8 x 0.25 + 5 = 7`. Reads apply the same decay without writing.

details.q: A bot clicks one product 5,000 times in a minute and it tops the trending list. What fixes this class of problem?
details.a: The weights are fine; the input is unbounded. Cap or dampen per-user, per-item repeats (`log(1+n)` or a hard cap) and deduplicate by event id. A shorter half-life only makes the spike fade sooner.

details.q: In what order do the stages go, and why?
details.a: Dedupe, cap, weight, decay, then rank. Dedupe and caps must come first so a duplicate or spammy event never contributes to the score; ranking is last because it only reads finished scores.

Only when events are measured on the same scale and window: the same weights, the same decay, the same event sources. A new event type or a changed half-life shifts every score, so version the scoring function and recompute or migrate rather than mixing.

prompts.q: Explain weighted event scoring and why it beats counting events.
points: Events have unequal value, so score = sum of weight x decay
Counts rank by volume, weights rank by value
Decay makes recent events matter more
Weights are product decisions tuned against outcomes

prompts.q: Show how to maintain a decayed score without keeping event history.
points: On event: score = score x 0.5^(dt/H) + weight
Apply the same decay when reading
Same idea as a lazily refilled token bucket

prompts.q: Make a trending-items score robust to bots and duplicates.
points: Dedupe by event id because delivery is at-least-once
Weight after capping, then decay, then rank
Keep scores on the same scale and window
